paragraphs.heading: The first wave to arrive
paragraphs.text: A P wave is one of the two main kinds of body wave, the seismic waves that travel through the inside of the Earth. P waves move faster than any other seismic wave. That is why they are the first signal from an earthquake to reach a seismograph or any place the quake affects. They can pass through gases and liquids as well as solids.

paragraphs.heading: Two meanings of one letter
paragraphs.text: The P can stand for pressure, because the wave is made of alternating squeezes and stretches of the material. It can also stand for primary, because its high speed makes it the first wave a seismograph records. In an even, uniform solid, a P wave runs in a straight line. The particles of the solid shake back and forth along the same line the wave is travelling.

paragraphs.heading: What sets the speed
paragraphs.text: A P wave's speed depends on how hard the material is to compress, how hard it is to shear, and how dense it is. Inside the Earth, density changes much less than the other two, so they mostly control the speed. In earthquakes, P waves usually travel at 5 to 8 km/s. In the crust they move at under 6 km/s; the lower mantle speeds them up to 13.5 km/s, and through the inner core they go about 11 km/s.

paragraphs.heading: Mapping the deep Earth
paragraphs.text: Seismologists watch how P and S waves behave to work out Earth's interior. Waves from a single quake take different routes, and the differences in when they arrive allow the inner structure to be mapped. Sudden jumps in speed at certain depths point to changes in phase or composition. Nearly everything known about the deep interior comes from studying body waves like these, or from the planet's normal modes.

paragraphs.heading: The P wave shadow zone
paragraphs.text: P waves do travel through Earth's liquid outer core, but they bend slightly as they cross from the semisolid mantle into it. As a result, there is a shadow zone between 103° and 142° from the quake's focus. In that band, seismometers do not pick up the first P waves.

paragraphs.heading: Seconds of warning
paragraphs.text: Because P waves cause little damage and outrun the destructive S and Rayleigh waves, detecting them can give advance warning of shaking. The warning ranges from mere seconds to roughly 60 to 90 seconds for large quakes that are deep and distant, like the 2011 Tohoku earthquake. Automated systems can use that time to send alerts, stop elevators at the nearest floor and shut off utilities. To work well, they must tell real P waves apart from local shaking caused by trucks or construction.
